slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/4
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum or plasma)  ·  Units: pg/mL, pmol/L

What it is used for: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) gives the body energy and helps keep nerves and blood cells healthy. B12 and folate (B9) are often measured together in a vitamin B12 and folate test, which is often used for symptoms of certain types of anemia.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/4
bullets: Symptoms of low B12 include fatigue, arrhythmia, unplanned weight loss, and tingly or numb hands and feet (a sign of nerve problems). Testing may also be done without symptoms when there are risk factors: celiac or Crohn’s disease, alcohol use disorder, malabsorption, not eating animal products (meat, eggs, dairy), digestive surgery including weight-loss surgery, and certain medicines that affect B vitamins.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/4
bullets: Physiology: Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble vitamin; because it contains cobalt, its compounds are called cobalamins. It is required for the development, myelination and function of the central nervous system, healthy red blood cell formation and DNA synthesis. B12 is a cofactor for two enzymes: methionine synthase (which converts homocysteine to methionine) and L-methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA).

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 4/4
bullets: The body does not make vitamin B12, so it must come from food or supplements. In food, B12 is bound to protein: stomach acid and enzymes free it, then in the duodenum it combines with intrinsic factor, made by the stomach’s parietal cells, and is absorbed in the distal ileum. B12 added to fortified foods and supplements is already in free form.

Range where checking MMA is suggested to confirm
No specific population stated in the source — 111–294 pmol/L. Expert suggestion cited by ODS.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: Large amounts of B vitamins in the body can also cause health problems or be due to an underlying condition such as liver disease. No tolerable upper intake level has been set for B12 because of its low potential for toxicity.

Low: The hallmark of vitamin B12 deficiency is megaloblastic anemia (large, abnormally nucleated red blood cells), along with low white cell, red cell and platelet counts, glossitis, fatigue, palpitations, pale skin, dementia, weight loss and infertility. Neurological changes such as numbness and tingling in the hands and feet can occur without anemia, so early diagnosis is important to avoid irreversible damage.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: Causes of deficiency include difficulty absorbing B12 from food, lack of intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia, the most common cause of clinically evident B12 deficiency), gastrointestinal surgery, long-term use of metformin or proton pump inhibitors, low dietary intake (e.g., a strict vegetarian or vegan diet), heavy alcohol use, celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, Helicobacter pylori infection and some inherited conditions (Imerslund–Gräsbeck syndrome).
Low: The body stores about 1 to 5 mg of vitamin B12 (about 1,000 to 2,000 times the usual daily intake), so symptoms of deficiency can take several years to appear.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/4
bullets: Pre-analytics: You may need to fast for several hours before a vitamin B blood test.
Interferences: Vitamin B results are not always clear-cut: inflammation in the body and certain medicines can affect them, and different labs have different normal ranges.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/4
bullets: During pregnancy, serum vitamin B12 levels tend to drop, sometimes to subnormal levels, but they usually return to normal after delivery.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/4
bullets: Limitations: The cutoff between normal B12 and deficiency varies by method and laboratory; most laboratories define subnormal values as below 200 or 250 pg/mL (148 or 185 pmol/L). Methylmalonic acid (MMA) is the most sensitive marker of B12 status; homocysteine also rises quickly as B12 declines, but has poor specificity (low folate and especially declining kidney function affect it).

slides.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/4
bullets: Vitamin B12–deficiency anemia is possible even when B12 levels are normal. The NHLBI table lists 400 pg/mL or higher as normal and 200 pg/mL or lower as deficiency for adults (although levels may be normal in some cases). If there are symptoms but the result is normal, other tests may be needed to make a diagnosis.

slides.title: Folate (vitamin B9, folic acid)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum); red blood cell folate may also be measured  ·  Units: ng/mL, nmol/L

What it is used for: B9 (folate or folic acid) helps the body make healthy new cells. Folate and B12 are often measured together, and a vitamin B12 and folate test is often used for symptoms of certain types of anemia.

slides.title: Folate (vitamin B9, folic acid)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Groups at risk of folate inadequacy include people with alcohol use disorder (alcohol interferes with folate absorption and hepatic uptake, speeds its breakdown and increases its renal excretion); women who can become pregnant (risk of neural tube defects); pregnant women (needs increase); and people with malabsorptive disorders (tropical sprue, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease; atrophic gastritis or gastric surgery).

slides.title: Folate (vitamin B9, folic acid)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Physiology: Folate (formerly folacin, sometimes vitamin B9) is the generic term for natural food folates and the folates in supplements and fortified foods, including folic acid. It acts as a coenzyme in single-carbon transfers in the synthesis of DNA and RNA and in amino acid metabolism — for example, converting homocysteine to methionine and making thymidylate, which is required for proper cell division. Impairment of this reaction can lead to megaloblastic anemia.
The total body content of folate is about 15 to 30 mg; about half is in the liver and the rest in blood and body tissues. The main form of folate in plasma is 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF).

slides.title: Folate (vitamin B9, folic acid)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: Large amounts of B vitamins in the body can also cause health problems or be due to an underlying condition such as liver disease.

Low: Isolated folate deficiency is uncommon; it usually coexists with other nutrient deficiencies because of its strong link with poor diet, alcoholism and malabsorptive disorders. Megaloblastic anemia is the primary clinical sign of folate or B12 deficiency (weakness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, headache, palpitations, shortness of breath). Soreness and shallow ulcers of the tongue and mouth, changes in skin, hair or fingernail pigmentation, gastrointestinal symptoms and raised blood homocysteine can also occur.

slides.title: Folate (vitamin B9, folic acid)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: Women with insufficient folate intakes are at increased risk of having babies with neural tube defects; inadequate maternal folate status has also been associated with low birth weight, preterm delivery and fetal growth retardation.

slides.title: Folate (vitamin B9, folic acid)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: You may need to fast for several hours before a vitamin B blood test.

Interferences: Some medicines affect folate status: antiepileptic drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate) can reduce serum folate; sulfasalazine inhibits folate absorption and can cause deficiency; methotrexate is a folate antagonist.
Serum folate is sensitive to recent dietary intake, so it might not reflect long-term status; red blood cell (erythrocyte) folate is a longer-term measure of folate intake.

slides.title: Folate (vitamin B9, folic acid)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: Large amounts of folate can correct the megaloblastic anemia, but not the neurological damage, of vitamin B12 deficiency. Experts have therefore been concerned that high-dose folate supplements might mask B12 deficiency until its neurological consequences become irreversible; the concern has now shifted to large amounts of folate possibly worsening the anemia and cognitive symptoms of B12 deficiency.

Plasma homocysteine is used as a functional indicator of folate status, but it is not highly specific, because kidney dysfunction and deficiencies of vitamin B12 and other micronutrients also influence it.

slides.title: Homocysteine
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (plasma)  ·  Units: µmol/L

What it is used for: Most often used to assess vitamin B6, B12 and folic acid status: a lack of any of them can raise homocysteine. Deficiencies of these vitamins can lead to anemia, nerve damage and cognitive decline. The test is also used to help diagnose homocystinuria (a rare genetic disease in which the body cannot make an enzyme that breaks down homocysteine) and to better understand heart attack or stroke risk in people who already have increased risk.

slides.title: Homocysteine
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: It may be ordered with symptoms of low B12 or folate: dizziness, fatigue or weakness, headache, heart palpitations, changes in skin or nail colour, sores on the tongue or in the mouth, and tingling or numbness in the hands, feet, arms or legs. Risk groups include malnutrition, older age and alcohol or drug addiction. It may also be ordered after a heart attack or stroke, with risk factors such as high LDL or high blood pressure, and in homocystinuria.

slides.title: Homocysteine
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Physiology: Homocysteine is an amino acid. Levels are normally low because the body uses vitamin B12, vitamin B6 and folic acid (folate) to quickly change it into other substances it needs. High homocysteine may be a sign that this process is not working or that certain B vitamins are lacking. Homocysteine that is not broken down can build up in arteries, damage them and increase the risk of blood clots, which may raise the risk of heart attack, stroke and other heart and blood vessel disorders.
Homocysteine levels rise when the body cannot convert homocysteine to methionine because of a 5-MTHF (folate) deficiency.

slides.title: Homocysteine
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: A high homocysteine level may mean not getting enough vitamin B12 or folic acid in the diet, homocystinuria (more testing is needed to confirm it) or a higher risk of heart disease, stroke or other blood vessel disorders. Homocysteine may also be higher with osteoporosis, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer’s disease or other dementias.

slides.title: Homocysteine
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/4
bullets: Pre-analytics: You may need to fast for 8 to 12 hours before the test. Some medicines and supplements may affect the results, so tell the provider about everything you take, especially B vitamins, but do not stop any medicine unless told to.

slides.title: Homocysteine
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/4
bullets: Interferences: Results may be affected by age (homocysteine may rise with age), sex (usually higher in males; it increases in females after menopause) and smoking; a high result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Homocysteine
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/4
bullets: Limitations: Routine homocysteine testing to screen for heart disease risk is not recommended for everyone, because it is uncertain how much homocysteine affects heart and blood vessel disease: studies have shown that in most cases lowering homocysteine does not reduce the risk of heart attack or stroke.

slides.title: Homocysteine
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/4
bullets: Homocysteine is not specific: declining kidney function and deficiencies of B12, folate and other micronutrients all influence it. Cut-offs also vary: 16 µmol/L is the most commonly used cut-off for elevated homocysteine (12–14 µmol/L have also been used), while in the context of B12 deficiency a value above 15 µmol/L is given as suggesting deficiency.

slides.title: Methylmalonic acid (MMA)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood or urine; heel-prick blood in newborn screening  ·  Units: µmol/L

What it is used for: An MMA test is most often used to diagnose vitamin B12 deficiency. It is also usually part of newborn screening, checking for methylmalonic acidemia — a rare genetic disorder (vomiting, dehydration, developmental delays, intellectual disability).

Serum MMA is the most sensitive marker of vitamin B12 status. Experts suggest checking serum MMA when serum B12 is between 150 and 399 pg/mL (111 to 294 pmol/L) to help confirm a diagnosis of deficiency.

slides.title: Methylmalonic acid (MMA)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Ordered with symptoms of B12 deficiency: fatigue, diarrhea, dizziness, shortness of breath, loss of appetite, tingling in the hands and/or feet, mood changes, confusion, irritability and pale skin. Risk is higher in strict vegetarians or vegans, with celiac or Crohn’s disease, alcohol use disorder, age over 75, Sjögren’s syndrome and after certain stomach or intestinal surgery.

Physiology: MMA is a substance made in small amounts when protein is digested. Vitamin B12 helps break MMA down into substances used in metabolism; without enough B12, more MMA is made than is broken down. So high MMA can be a sign of vitamin B12 deficiency.

slides.title: Methylmalonic acid (MMA)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Biochemical basis: B12 is a cofactor for L-methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the metabolism of propionate.

slides.title: Methylmalonic acid (MMA)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Reference values and decision limits
rows: No specific population stated in the source — MMA can be higher with renal insufficiency and in older adults.

slides.title: Methylmalonic acid (MMA)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result
cols: Higher than normal MMA may mean vitamin B12 deficiency, but the test cannot show how severe it is; to diagnose, the result is compared with a homocysteine test and/or vitamin B tests. In a baby, moderate or high MMA may mean methylmalonic acidemia, which can cause life-threatening complications if untreated.
Lower than normal MMA levels are not common and are not considered a health problem.

slides.title: Methylmalonic acid (MMA)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: MMA may be measured in blood or urine (a 24-hour or random sample); newborn screening uses a few drops of blood from the heel. You may need to fast for several hours before the test.
Interferences: MMA levels also rise with renal insufficiency and tend to be higher in older adults.
Limitations: The provider interprets the result together with symptoms, medical history and other blood tests.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: fL

What it is used for: MCV is usually part of a complete blood count. Because each type of anemia affects red cell size, shape and quality differently, MCV helps identify the type of anemia together with other tests.
Physiology: MCV measures the average size of red blood cells. Cells that are too small or too large may be a sign of anemia, a lack of certain vitamins or other conditions.
NHLBI reports MCV in femtoliters (fL); a femtoliter is a measure of volume.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: Larger-than-normal red cells may be a sign of pernicious anemia (from a lack of vitamin B12 or a disease that affects its use, such as certain autoimmune diseases, celiac disease or Crohn’s disease), anemia from a lack of folic acid, or liver disease.

Red cells that are smaller than normal may be a sign of certain anemias, including iron deficiency anemia (the most common form), or of thalassemia (a group of inherited disorders with fewer healthy red cells and less hemoglobin, which can cause severe anemia).

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Interferences: Age, diet, activity level, medicines, menstrual period and other conditions can affect MCV; an abnormal value does not always need treatment.

MCV can be falsely high with cold agglutinins, hyperglycaemia and prolonged sample storage (red cells swell; Dolgov et al. cite storage longer than 8 hours). Severe hyponatraemia can falsely lower it. A sudden change that does not fit previous results suggests an error.
Limitations: MCV alone cannot diagnose a disease. Anemia can occur with a normal MCV — for example, after sudden blood loss, in kidney failure or in aplastic anemia.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Read MCV together with RDW: low MCV with normal RDW — uniform microcytosis (thalassaemia trait, some anaemia of chronic disease); low MCV with high RDW — iron deficiency likely (check ferritin and transferrin saturation); normal MCV with high RDW — mixed populations (early iron deficiency, combined iron + B12/folate deficiency, after transfusion). The reticulocyte count separates poor production from loss or destruction.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Overview
bullets: Vitamin B12–deficiency anemia can result from lack of intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia), intestinal conditions, stomach or intestinal surgery, certain medicines (such as metformin and some heartburn medicines), heavy alcohol use or a strict vegetarian diet.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Tests to consider · 1/2
rows: A complete blood count measures hemoglobin.
Vitamin B12 level; B12 and folate are often measured together.
Measured with B12 when there are symptoms of certain types of anemia.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Tests to consider · 2/2
rows: Most often used to diagnose B12 deficiency; high MMA can be a sign of deficiency.
Most often used to check for B12 and folate deficiency: it rises when B6, B12 or folic acid is low.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Result patterns
rows: B12-deficiency anemia is likely; more tests may be needed to find the cause.
B12 normal but symptoms present; MMA ↑
B12 deficiency is still possible — a normal B12 level does not rule it out.
Possible lack of B12 or folic acid (also homocystinuria and other conditions).
Heterogeneous macrocytosis — B12 or folate deficiency, myelodysplasia possible.

slides.title: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Cautions
bullets: Inflammation and certain medicines can affect results; laboratories use different reference ranges.

slides.title: 1. Is there anaemia?
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Defined by haemoglobin. WHO (2024): <120 g/L in non-pregnant women aged 15–65, <130 g/L in men; cut-offs are adjusted for age, pregnancy, altitude and smoking.
First check that the result is genuine — see “Analyser spurious results”.

slides.title: 2. Type by MCV
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Low MCV (≈ <80 fL): Microcytic: mostly iron deficiency; thalassaemia → ferritin, iron studies
Normal MCV: Normocytic: acute blood loss, kidney disease, chronic disease, aplastic anaemia → reticulocytes decide
High MCV (≈ >100 fL): Macrocytic: B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease, alcohol, hypothyroidism → B12, folate

slides.title: 3. Marrow response — reticulocytes
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: High (≈ >80×10⁹/L): Bleeding, haemolysis or recovery after treatment → haemolysis markers
Low (≈ <20×10⁹/L with severe anaemia): Poor production: deficiencies, kidney, marrow disease
Cut-offs are approximate; use the absolute count or a corrected index (CRC, RPI) rather than the percentage.

slides.title: MCV with RDW
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: MCV ↓, RDW normal: Thalassaemia trait, some anaemia of chronic disease
MCV ↓, RDW ↑: Iron deficiency (ferritin, transferrin saturation)
MCV normal, RDW ↑: Early iron deficiency, mixed deficiency, after transfusion
MCV ↑, RDW ↑: B12 or folate deficiency, myelodysplasia

slides.title: Iron: deficiency or inflammation?
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Iron deficiency: Ferritin ↓, iron ↓, transferrin saturation ↓, TIBC usually ↑
Anaemia of inflammation: Iron ↓, TIBC ↓, ferritin normal or ↑
Ferritin cut-off (WHO 2020): Healthy adults <15 µg/L; with inflammation <70 µg/L (with CRP, AGP)

slides.title: Haemolysis markers
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Reticulocytes ↑, LDH ↑, indirect bilirubin ↑, haptoglobin ↓.
The Coombs (antiglobulin) test identifies immune haemolysis; spherocytes suggest a membrane defect, schistocytes thrombotic microangiopathy.
A marked LDH rise with haemosiderinuria — intravascular haemolysis.

slides.title: Hypersegmented neutrophil
slides.eyebrow: Differential · cells
slides.caption:
Size: Often larger than a normal neutrophil
Nucleus: 5–10 lobes
Cytoplasm: As in a normal neutrophil
Granules: Fine, mauve
Key feature: Count the lobes: 5 or more.
Seen in: Macrocytic anaemia from folate or vitamin B12 deficiency.

slides.title: A symptomatic patient has serum B12 = 184 pmol/L (250 pg/mL). According to ODS, which test is suggested to confirm the diagnosis?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. MMA is the most sensitive B12 marker, though it also rises with renal insufficiency.

Basis: With B12 of 111–294 pmol/L (150–399 pg/mL), experts suggest checking serum methylmalonic acid (MMA).

slides.title: Why is B12 checked along with folate when looking for the cause of anemia?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Because folate destroys B12 in the blood
Folate may hide the anemia but leave the nerve damage
Because both are always measured with one reagent in one tube
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. So some experts have been concerned that large amounts of folate might mask B12 deficiency until its neurological effects become irreversible (the question is not fully settled).

Basis: Large amounts of folate correct the megaloblastic anemia of B12 deficiency, but not the nerve damage.

slides.title: MCV is low (small red cells). Which causes does the source give?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Small cells: iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia. Large: B12/folate deficiency, liver disease.

slides.title: MCV is normal. Does that rule out anemia?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Yes, a normal MCV rules it out
No, e.g. after sudden blood loss
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Anemia can occur with a normal MCV: sudden blood loss, kidney failure, aplastic anemia.

slides.title: MCV 72 fL with a high RDW. Which test comes next in the anaemia algorithm?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Heterogeneous microcytosis suggests iron deficiency — ferritin and transferrin saturation.

slides.title: Erythropoiesis (normoblastic, megaloblastic). Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the erythroid lineage?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/3
bullets: 1. Erythropoiesis in the bone marrow: hematopoietic stem cell → common myeloid progenitor → erythroid progenitors; the main humoral regulator is erythropoietin, produced in the kidney in response to hypoxia (enhances survival and division of progenitors).

2. Normoblastic (normal) lineage: proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatophilic → orthochromic (oxyphilic) erythroblast → nucleus extruded → reticulocyte → erythrocyte. During maturation the cell becomes smaller, the nucleus condenses, hemoglobin accumulates in the cytoplasm, and basophilia is replaced by oxyphilia.

slides.title: Erythropoiesis (normoblastic, megaloblastic). Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the erythroid lineage?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/3
bullets: 3. The reticulocyte matures in the bone marrow for ~1–3 days and in the blood for ~1–2 days; the mature erythrocyte is an anucleate biconcave disc, circulates for ~120 days and is destroyed by splenic macrophages.
4. Erythrocyte function: transport of O2 and CO2 via hemoglobin; its shape and membrane provide deformability.

5. Megaloblastic erythropoiesis – in B12 or folate deficiency DNA synthesis is impaired: nuclear maturation lags behind the cytoplasm (nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony), the cells are large (megaloblasts), erythropoiesis is ineffective – many cells die in the bone marrow itself.

slides.title: Erythropoiesis (normoblastic, megaloblastic). Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the erythroid lineage?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 3/3
bullets: 6. In the megaloblastic state, the peripheral blood shows macrocytosis (MCV >100 fL) and hypersegmented neutrophils; in the postnatal period this is always a sign of pathology.

slides.title: Anemias related to vitamin B12 deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Causes: pernicious anemia (antibodies to intrinsic factor or parietal cells – B12 is not absorbed), gastrectomy, ileal disease/resection, vegetarian diet, drugs (metformin, nitrous oxide), parasite (fish tapeworm).

2. Mechanism: B12 is a cofactor of methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; in deficiency DNA synthesis is impaired → megaloblastic erythropoiesis, homocysteine and MMA rise.

3. Clinical: anemia, glossitis, jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis/hemolysis), neurological disturbances (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, neuropathy, cognitive impairment) – may occur even without anemia.

slides.title: Anemias related to vitamin B12 deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Laboratory: macrocytic anemia (MCV >100), hypersegmented neutrophils, often leuko- and thrombocytopenia; B12 <200 pg/mL – deficiency, 200–300 – borderline (measure MMA and homocysteine); MMA is more specific for B12 deficiency (normal in folate deficiency).
5. Confirming pernicious anemia: antibodies to intrinsic factor (specific), antibodies to parietal cells; the Schilling test is no longer performed.
6. A rise in reticulocytes 3–5 days after treatment confirms the diagnosis; differentiate from folate deficiency.

slides.title: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias related to vitamin B12 deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Peripheral blood: macrocytic (MCV >100 fL) hyperchromic anemia, macro-ovalocytes, anisopoikilocytosis, Howell-Jolly bodies and Cabot rings may be present; neutrophils are hypersegmented (≥5 lobes).
2. Often pancytopenia (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia); reticulocytes low (ineffective erythropoiesis).
3. Bone marrow: hypercellular, erythroid hyperplasia, megaloblasts – large cells, nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony (nucleus "young", cytoplasm hemoglobinized); giant metamyelocytes and bands.

slides.title: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias related to vitamin B12 deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Biochemistry: signs of ineffective erythropoiesis/intramedullary destruction – LDH and indirect bilirubin increased; B12 low, MMA and homocysteine high.
5. Bone marrow examination is usually not required – vitamins and metabolites suffice; if necessary it is taken before treatment starts (megaloblastosis disappears quickly after treatment).
